questions.question: Q: How did housing differ between rich and poor Romans?
questions.correctAnswer: The wealthy lived in domus — spacious single-family houses with gardens and private facilities. The poor lived in insulae — cramped, multi-storey blocks with shared facilities, no running water and high fire risk.

questions.question: Q: Why were the Roman baths so important socially?
questions.correctAnswer: They were not just for washing — they were community centres for exercise, socialising, conducting business, relaxing and even studying. Going to the baths was a daily ritual for most Romans.

questions.question: Q: What did ordinary Romans eat?
questions.correctAnswer: Breakfast (ientaculum) was bread and cheese; lunch (prandium) was light — leftovers or street food; dinner (cena) was the main meal — porridge, vegetables, bread and occasionally meat or fish for those who could afford it.

questions.question: Q: What was the role of the paterfamilias in family life?
questions.correctAnswer: He had legal authority over the entire household, arranged marriages, controlled finances and made major decisions. His power was theoretically absolute but in practice moderated by social expectations.

questions.question: Q: How reliable was Rome's water supply?
questions.correctAnswer: Very reliable by ancient standards — aqueducts brought fresh water from miles away, feeding public fountains, baths and some private homes. The Cloaca Maxima drained waste water, making Rome remarkably hygienic.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response How far did wealth determine the quality of daily life in Rome? (15 marks) <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Wealth was the single most important factor determining the quality of daily life in Rome, shaping every aspect from housing and food to health and leisure. The contrast between the rich in their domus and the poor in their insulae was stark: wealthy Romans enjoyed spacious homes with gardens, private baths, fresh water and slave servants, while the poor crowded into fire-prone apartment blocks with no cooking facilities, shared latrines and limited water access. Food divided the classes equally sharply — the wealthy ate elaborate multi-course cenae with imported delicacies, while the poor survived on bread, porridge and vegetables. Leisure was also class-dependent: the elite enjoyed private villas and exclusive entertainments, while the poor relied on free public games and the baths for recreation. However, some aspects of Roman life were more egalitarian. The public baths were accessible to all citizens for a small fee, providing exercise and social interaction regardless of wealth. The grain dole (annona) ensured that even the poor received basic food. Public entertainments in the Colosseum and Circus Maximus were free. The legal system theoretically applied equally to all citizens. Yet even these 'equal' provisions reinforced status — the elite sat in the best seats at games, and wealth bought better legal representation.
